Measurement report · August 2026 · revised October 2026

Retry Backoff Under Failure

What 72 controlled runs say about delivery, latency, and the thundering herd in a queue-based delivery engine.

Swati Bhatt 72 runs · 6 strategies · 2 failure regimes github.com/swati-bhatt/syncin

Abstract

We measure how the choice of retry-backoff strategy affects delivery reliability, latency, and provider load in a queue-based delivery engine, under two failure regimes: steady per-call transient failure and a full provider outage. Six strategies (immediate, fixed, exponential, and the full, equal and decorrelated jitter variants as named and compared by Brooker, 2015) share the same base and cap (1 s, 15 s) and, within each regime, the same attempt budget. Under steady uncorrelated failure, strategy choice barely matters: delivery converges to ≈ 1−fⁿ and cost to ≈ 1/(1−f) calls per delivery regardless of waits — waiting only adds tail latency. Under a correlated outage the ranking inverts and separates sharply. The mock provider fails every call until it has been up for 60 s; our synchronized cohort of 100 reminders made its first attempt about 26 s after boot, so it faced an effective outage of W ≈ 34 s. With 8 attempts, immediate and fixed retry deliver 0%, full jitter 32%, decorrelated 73%, and exponential 100%. Survival is governed by schedule coverage — whether the sum of a job's waits reaches W — and a Monte Carlo of the engine's own backoff function predicts all six outcomes from that rule alone (full jitter: 33% predicted, 32% observed). Equal jitter keeps half of each exponential wait as a floor; at this outage length it matched exponential's 100% with a ~5× smaller recovery peak (15–23 attempts in the busiest second, against exponential's 100). The same model predicts that this tie does not carry over to a true 60 s window at this budget: there, full and equal jitter both fall to ≈ 0%. We argue that backoff should be sized as a deadline-coverage problem first and jittered above a floor second; the second half rests on one measured outage length.

01System under test

Syncin is a multi-tenant scheduled-delivery engine (Node/Fastify · PostgreSQL/Prisma · Redis/BullMQ). Creating an event transactionally persists reminder rows, then enqueues delayed jobs; a worker (concurrency 5) delivers each due reminder through a provider interface, retrying failures on a configurable backoff schedule and dead-lettering after a fixed attempt budget. Idempotency is enforced at every hop — request, schedule, send and reply. Under the queue's at-least-once semantics, a redelivered job skips any reminder whose send is already recorded. A crash after the provider accepts a send but before the engine commits it can still re-send: the reminder id is passed to the provider as its idempotency key, so a provider that dedupes could close that window, but the mock does not, and no real adapter exists yet. Two concurrent runs of one reminder (e.g. a manual redeliver while the original job is active) can also both send, because the send check is check-then-act.

The provider is an in-process mock with configurable failure injection: per-call failure probability and a transient/permanent split (random and unseeded, so re-runs reproduce rates, not exact counts), added latency, and a deterministic “provider outage until uptime T” mode. Every provider attempt is recorded with a millisecond timestamp and exposed via /metrics/attempts; engine state via /metrics.

StrategyWait before attempt n+1 (n = attempts made so far)
none0

exponentialmin(cap, b·2ⁿ⁻¹) = exp
full jitterU(0, exp)
equal jitterexp/2 + U(0, exp/2)

b = base (1 s); cap = 15 s; waits are floored to whole milliseconds. Full, equal and decorrelated jitter are the variants as named and compared by Brooker (2015); Syncin's implementations follow his definitions, with the attempt index shifted by one. Unknown strategy names fall back to full jitter.

02Method

Each run executes on an isolated stack — its own Docker Compose project, ports, and fresh database volumes — created and destroyed per run. A run fires N = 100 reminders whose due time is the same instant (about 40 s after creation in the steady runs, 25 s in the outage runs), so failure and retry cohorts are synchronized: the worst case for herd effects, and the fair case for comparing strategies. The run ends when no reminder remains in a non-terminal state; we then collect terminal states, per-delivery latency, engine metrics, and the raw provider attempt log.

Scenarios

  • Steady transient failure. Each provider call fails independently with probability f ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}; attempt budget 5. Three repeats per (strategy, f).
  • Provider outage (effective W ≈ 34 s). The mock provider fails every call until it has been up for 60 s, then recovers fully; attempt budget 8. The reminders were scheduled 25 s after creation, so the synchronized cohort made its first attempt about 26 s after boot and faced an effective outage of W ≈ 34 s, not 60 s. Three repeats per strategy.

Effective outage window

The outage is keyed to the provider's process uptime, not to the reminders' due time, so we measure the window the cohort actually faced. In the jittered runs, attempts are dense around recovery, so the last failed and the first successful attempt bracket it: across those nine runs, recovery fell 32.6–34.5 s after the cohort's first attempt (median bracket midpoint W = 33.6 s), which puts that first attempt at about 26 s of uptime. At budget 8, exponential's waits reach 45 s by attempt 7 and 60 s by attempt 8; full jitter's expected reach is ≈ 30 s (sd ≈ 8 s); equal jitter's lies between 30 s and just under 60 s (mean ≈ 45 s).

Coverage model

A job survives the outage if and only if the sum of its waits is at least W, so that its last attempt lands at or after recovery. We estimate P(Σ waits ≥ W) for each strategy by Monte Carlo (400,000 trials, fixed seed), replicating the engine's computeBackoff exactly, millisecond floors included. Assumptions: waits only — per-attempt processing time and worker queueing are ignored, which delays attempts slightly and so helps survival a little; W comes from the jittered runs' recovery bracket; every job starts at the cohort's first attempt. A prediction agrees with a measurement when the pooled observation (n = 300) lies within the prediction over the bracket, widened by 2 binomial standard errors.

Recovery load

Peak recovery load is the most provider attempts in any 1-second sliding window at or after the cohort's first successful delivery. Because the strategies reach recovery with very different numbers of live jobs, we also report it per surviving job (peak ÷ delivered).

Injection validity

Pooled over all 54 steady runs (7,995 provider calls), observed failure rates were 0.106 / 0.296 / 0.488 against configured 0.1 / 0.3 / 0.5, each within 1.35 binomial standard errors. Delivery also matched expectation: at f = 0.5 with 5 attempts, the expected 1−0.5⁵ = 96.9% against 96–98% observed (cell means; pooled 97.3%).

03Results

3.1 Steady failure: strategy choice barely matters

Every strategy's mean delivery was 96–100% at every failure rate (single runs 91–100%; the lowest, one fixed-retry run at f = 0.5, saw an observed failure fraction of 0.573). Provider cost is equally flat: 1.08–1.16 calls per delivered message at f = 0.1 and 1.85–2.09 at f = 0.5 across all six — with independent per-call failure, expected attempts per delivery is 1/(1−f) no matter how long you wait.

What waiting does change is latency. Immediate retry resolves everything sub-second even at f = 0.5 (p99 0.85 s), while exponential and decorrelated drag p99 to 15.6 s and 16.9 s; full jitter cuts exponential's p95 tail to about a third (3.9 s vs 11.1 s), with equal jitter in between (5.7 s). Immediate retry has the lowest p99 at every failure rate, but not the lowest median: at f = 0.1 it is fifth of six at p50 (0.55 s, against full jitter's 0.26 s).

Peak recovery load = the most provider attempts in any 1-second sliding window at or after the cohort's first successful delivery; per surviving job = peak ÷ delivered. In every run, all failed calls came before the first success, that is, during the outage.

Immediate retry spends all 8 attempts within ~1 s (800 failed calls, peaking at 594–772 attempts in a 1-second window); fixed lasts 7 s. Both go extinct long before recovery. Exponential's deterministic schedule reaches 45 s by attempt 7 and 60 s by attempt 8, so it outlasts W: every job succeeded on attempt 7, with one attempt to spare. But its retries stay in lockstep. The pulse at 30 s still falls inside the outage, and the next one, at 45 s, arrives about 12 s after recovery (11–13 s, allowing for the bracket), with the whole cohort landing within about half a second (0.36–0.60 s). The provider had already recovered; the wave is simply the first traffic it sees. Full jitter draws each wait from U(0, exp), halving the expected reach to ≈ 30 s, just short of W: only 32% survive (the model in §3.4 predicts 33%). It did not spare the provider either: during the outage it sent more calls than exponential (762 vs 600 before the first success, mean of 3 runs), with about twice the 1-second peak (199 vs 100). Its low recovery peak is partly attrition: only 26–38 jobs were still alive at recovery. Per surviving job (0.24–0.31 attempts) its jitter does spread arrivals compared with exponential's 1.0, but it is no calmer than equal jitter (0.15–0.23), so its peak is lower than equal jitter's only because fewer jobs survived.

3.3 Equal jitter: coverage and calm

Equal jitter keeps half of each exponential wait as a deterministic floor and randomizes only the upper half. It is not new: it is one of the three variants named and compared by Brooker (2015). Over 7 waits its guaranteed (worst-case) reach is 30 s from the floors, its expected reach ≈ 45 s, and its maximum just under 60 s. At this outage length (W ≈ 34 s) it survived 100% in all three runs, matching exponential, with a ~5× smaller recovery peak: 15–23 attempts in the busiest second (mean 18.7) against exponential's 100. Because exponential's whole cohort lands within about half a second, its 100 is capped by N, and the ratio would grow with a finer window. Equal jitter did not survive on its floor alone: 30 s falls short of W, so the random half had to add another 3.6 s (2.6–4.5 s across the recovery bracket), which the model says happens 99.95% of the time. Its steady-state profile stays mid-pack (p95 5.7 s at f = 0.5).

3.4 Schedule coverage predicts the outage ranking

If survival is schedule coverage, P(Σ waits ≥ W) should predict each strategy's delivery without reference to the runs. The coverage model (§02) does, for all six:

Model vs measurement. Predictions are a Monte Carlo of computeBackoff at 8 attempts (7 waits), 400,000 trials, counting waits only. The Σ-waits range is the Monte Carlo's for the jittered strategies. Every observation lies within its prediction over the bracket, widened by 2 binomial SE (n = 300).

The measured ranking is the one each schedule's arithmetic predicts at W ≈ 34 s. Fig 5 uses the same model to ask what was not measured: how survival changes with the length of the outage.

What about a true 60-second outage? By the model only: at W = 60 s, full jitter and equal jitter are both predicted to deliver ≈ 0%, decorrelated ≈ 28%, and exponential sits exactly at its boundary — its 8th attempt lands at 60 s of waiting, so 60 s is the longest window it covers. Equal jitter's floors reach 60 s only with 12 attempts (11 waits), and decorrelated's predicted survival overtakes equal jitter's from W ≈ 44.7 s. Equal jitter's tie with exponential is therefore a result about this outage length and this budget, not a general one.

The mechanism

Outage survival is schedule coverage — whether the sum of your backoff waits reaches the outage the cohort actually faces. Full jitter halves that sum in expectation, giving up half of the client's outage tolerance; a floor under the jitter keeps part of it.

04Discussion

Survival is a deadline-coverage problem

With a fixed attempt budget, what decides outage survival is whether the sum of backoff waits reaches the outage the cohort faces. Jitter drawn from [0, exp] halves that sum in expectation — so full jitter, whose purpose is protecting the provider from herds, gives up about half the client's outage tolerance. Nothing about this is specific to our engine: it falls out of arithmetic on the schedule, and the measurements land where that arithmetic says they should (§3.4). The window that matters is measured from when the work comes due, not from when the fault began: here 60 s of configured downtime became W ≈ 34 s for the cohort.

Jitter above a floor, not across the interval

Jitter exists because retries that back off by the same amount collide again (Brooker, 2019). Retries during an overload can also keep load high after the original problem is fixed, delaying recovery (Brooker, 2019). Brooker (2015) named and compared full, equal and decorrelated jitter by simulating many clients contending to update one database row and retrying until they succeeded. In that setting full jitter did the least work, decorrelated jitter finished slightly sooner, and equal jitter took the longest of the jittered variants. This study's setting and metrics differ: a synchronized cohort facing a provider outage under a fixed attempt budget, judged by how many jobs outlast the outage and by the load they bring at recovery. There, equal jitter's floor of half of each exponential wait guarantees half of the exponential schedule's reach (30 s of 60 s here; full jitter guarantees none). At W ≈ 34 s that kept enough coverage, while its random half still de-synchronized the cohort.

The floor fraction is a dial between the two goals: raise it (e.g. 0.75·exp + U(0, 0.25·exp)) for more coverage and less smoothing, or lower it (e.g. 0.25·exp + U(0, 0.75·exp)) for more smoothing and less coverage. Neither variant was measured, and the floor is fixed at exp/2 in code today.

Steady-state failure is the wrong regime to tune for

Under uncorrelated failure, delivery and cost are attempt-count-driven and strategy-independent; aggressive retrying even gives the lowest p99 latency at every failure rate (and the lowest p95 at f ≥ 0.3), though not the lowest median. The regime that punishes bad backoff is the correlated one — outages — which is exactly the regime that synthetic “x% of requests fail” testing does not exercise. Failure injection should include outage shapes.

Practical sizing rule

We propose a rule, not a validated result: pick the outage you must survive, measured from when the work comes due; size the guaranteed sum of waits — the floor sum, Σ exp/2 for equal jitter — and the attempt budget to cover it; then add bounded jitter above the floor. The measured outage did not exercise this rule as stated: equal jitter's 30 s floor did not itself cover W, and survival relied on the random half. In this engine the rule is three environment variables (REMINDER_MAX_ATTEMPTS, REMINDER_BACKOFF_BASE_MS, REMINDER_BACKOFF_CAP_MS). On the strength of these results the engine's default strategy was switched from full jitter to equal jitter, but the default budget stayed at 5 attempts, which reaches only 7.5–15 s. Coverage scales with the attempt budget, so size those three to the outage you must survive.

05Threats to validity

  • Mock provider. Failures are synthetic and instantaneous; real providers exhibit latency correlated with failure, partial brown-outs, and rate limiting. The mock runs in-process, so “provider load” counts calls, not network cost.
  • Hypothesis after the fact. Equal jitter was added after we saw the first five strategies' outage results. It was evaluated on fresh runs, but in the same single scenario, and the engine default was switched on that evidence. Its 100% is not a held-out test.
  • Fixed attempt budget. Strategies are compared at equal attempt count, not equal expected wait, which favours long schedules. Given the same expected total wait as equal jitter (10 attempts, expected Σ = 45 s), full jitter's predicted survival at W ≈ 34 s is 86.78% (84.72–88.68% over the bracket), so its 32% describes full jitter at this budget, not full jitter in general.
  • One outage length. One effective window (W ≈ 34 s) was measured, with a synchronized cohort, the worst case for herds. Fig 5 extends it by model only; its crossovers, such as decorrelated overtaking equal jitter from W ≈ 44.7 s, are untested. W itself is inferred from the attempt logs, not recorded.
  • Single machine and run ordering. All stacks share one host. Each cell's three repeats ran concurrently on separate stacks, so a strategy's runs contended mainly with copies of itself; cells ran sequentially in strategy order; and equal jitter ran in a separate, later batch on a rebuilt image. Strategy is therefore confounded with time of run, and concurrent repeats are not fully independent, so within-cell spread may understate the true variance.
  • Scale. N = 100 × 3 repeats per cell. Near the delivery ceiling, differences below ~3 pp are not resolvable, so the 96–98% spread between strategies at f = 0.5 is within noise; in the outage regime the resolution is ~7 pp (full jitter's runs span 26–38%). These are binomial approximations, and between-run spread can exceed binomial noise, so the real thresholds are at least this large. p99 rests on ~3 observations per cell. Standard deviations are sample SDs.

06Reproducing

Raw per-run JSON — including full attempt-timestamp logs — is committed under experiments/results/raw/. experiments/analyze.py writes everything quoted here from those logs: the summary table (summary.md), the derived numbers and coverage model (derived.json, derived.md), and both figure sets. The sweep is resumable: run-one.sh skips any configuration whose result file exists, so on a fresh clone it re-runs nothing. To re-run the whole study from scratch (72 isolated runs, about an hour on a laptop), move the committed results aside first. Failure injection is unseeded, so a re-run reproduces rates, not exact counts.

mv experiments/results/raw experiments/results/raw.orig
mkdir experiments/results/raw
./experiments/sweep.sh 3                    # 72 isolated runs, resumable
pip install numpy matplotlib
python3 experiments/analyze.py              # summary, derived numbers, figures/
THEME=dark python3 experiments/analyze.py   # figures-dark/
